newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: German bankers see amicable end to Bonn-Buba spat.
newsitem.headline: German bankers see amicable end to Bonn-Buba spat.

text.p: Top German bankers on Tuesday predicted an amicable end to the tussle between Bonn and the Bundesbank over plans to revalue gold and currency reserves and downplayed the importance of hitting Maastricht targets dead centre.

"I am pretty sure the government is not interested in hurting the reputation of the Bundesbank or the other way around," Martin Kohlhaussen, chief executive of third-largest bank Commerzbank told Reuters.

Bayerische Vereinsbank chief executive Albrecht Schmidt said the split between the government and the German central bank was unnecessary, since it made no sense for Bonn to try to meet precise Maastricht Treaty criteria at any cost.
Like other bankers, he said Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) was still fully on track and praised EU countries' progress in reining in their debt and deficits for the euro.
"We are looking at the frame, not at the picture and the picture is one of a converging Europe," Schmidt said.
"We in the industry know that three percent is not necessarily 3.0 percent," he added.
Maastricht demands that countries taking part in the euro launch reduce their deficits to three percent of gross domestic product -- a key sticking point for Germany.
Bonn's asset revaluation plan, with proceeds to be used to retire old debt this year and next, is seen as boosting German chances of meeting monetary union criteria this year.

The Bundesbank has dismissed the plan as an assault on its autonomy and on Germany's credibility as a euro hardliner, and has recommended that the revaluation not take place until 1999, or until EMU participants are chosen in 1998 at the earliest.
Bankers conceded that the timing of the government's plan was unfortunate but said agreement would be reached.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer expressed optimism that a compromise could be reached after talks in Bonn on Tuesday.
The bankers were speaking on the fringes of the International Monetary Conference in Interlaken, Switzerland, where Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Monday defended the gold revaluation plan.
"This is nothing special. The gold is valued at very very low prices. I would not mind a revaluation," Kohlhaussen said.
The Bundesbank has some 95 million ounces of gold in its reserves, valued at 13.7 billion marks versus a current market value of more than 55 billion marks.
Confident that EMU was on track, Kohlhaussen said he favoured a euro launch involving as many participants as possible and said a broader-based currency union had the best chances of success.
Hilmar Kopper, former chief executive and now supervisory board chairman of Deutsche Bank said the Bundesbank's dispute with Bonn in no way threatened monetary union.
"The issue is not political, it is technical," Kopper said.
Separately, the Federal Association of German Banks said European Union members could still qualify for monetary union if they slightly exceeded the three percent deficit level.

"It would be politically and economically fatal if the project were to collapse if the German deficit was at 3.2 percent as recently predicted by the research institutes," the association's managing director, Manfred Weber, told a news conference in Frankfurt.
Weber said sustainable financial stability was more critical than hitting 3.0 percent precisely.
"Pointing this out has nothing to do with softening," Weber said. "That also applies against the backdrop of the French election outcome," Weber said.

However bankers expressed some concern over the announcement by the ruling French Socialist party to seek a renegotiation of the stability pact, which was agreed to ensure lasting fiscal discipline after monetary union.
Kohlhaussen said he would not be pleased at any changes to this agreement, while Kopper said he expected some talks to ocur on the issue, but did not fear any amendments.
"It is not unusual for a new government to want to address certain issues," Weber said. "The stability pact has been agreed and lays a solid foundation for monetary union."
--Zurich Newsroom, +41 1 631 7340
